notes.meaning: Paul reminds the Christians in Corinth about the gospel, the good news about Jesus that he had shared with them. They had welcomed this message, and it became the solid rock on which their daily faith stood.

Paul explains that this good news is the path to salvation if they keep holding firmly to the truth he taught them. If someone abandons the message or treats it like empty words, their initial faith accomplishes nothing. Real faith continues to cling to God's promise.

Paul did not make up this message, but received it from the Lord and passed it along as the truth of highest importance. The heart of the message is that Christ died for our sins to atone for our wrongdoing, taking the penalty we deserved so we could be reconciled to God. This death was not an accident, but happened in exact fulfillment of the Old Testament Scriptures.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that verses 3–7 record an early formal creed of the church, dating to within a couple of years after Jesus' death.

notes.meaning: Jesus was placed in a tomb, which proved beyond doubt that His human body had truly died. On the third day He was raised to life in a body that will never die again, just as the ancient prophecies had foretold. His empty grave serves as proof that God accepted His sacrifice.

After rising, Jesus appeared in person to Peter, and later to the Twelve apostles together. Calling the group the Twelve was their traditional title, even though Judas was no longer among them. This private visit offered comfort and restoration to Peter after his painful denial of Jesus.

Jesus also appeared to more than five hundred believers all gathered in one place, probably in Galilee. Most of those eyewitnesses were still alive when Paul wrote this letter, so any skeptic could question them directly. A few had fallen asleep, which was Paul's gentle way of describing the physical death of believers who will one day wake up.

Next, Jesus appeared privately to James, His earthly brother, who later became a prominent leader in the Jerusalem church. After that visit, the Lord showed Himself to all the apostles together before He was taken up into heaven. These personal meetings convinced formerly skeptical family members and disciples that He was alive.

Finally, the risen Lord appeared to Paul himself during his journey on the road to Damascus. Paul describes himself as one born abnormally late, like a child born at the wrong time, because his meeting with Christ happened after the ascension. He felt humbled that Jesus would reveal Himself to him in such a dramatic and unexpected way.

Paul looked upon himself as the least of all the apostles, not even worthy of bearing the title. He could never forget that he had violently hunted down and persecuted God's church before his conversion. That painful memory produced lifelong humility and gratitude for God's forgiveness.

Paul attributed everything he had become and accomplished entirely to God's grace, which means His free and unearned favor. That gift of grace was not wasted, for Paul traveled farther and worked harder than any other apostle. Even so, he refused to take credit, knowing God's power was doing the work through him.

It made no difference which apostle preached, whether Paul or the original twelve disciples. They all proclaimed the exact same foundational message about Christ's death and resurrection, and that is what the Corinthians had believed. The power is always in the message of God, not in the human messenger.

Since the apostles constantly preached that Christ rose from the dead, Paul asks how some in Corinth could claim that dead bodies never rise. Influenced by Greek philosophy, some members believed souls lived on after death, but they laughed at the thought of a physical resurrection. Paul begins to show how dangerous and contradictory that idea really was.

Paul uses clear logic to expose their error. If the physical resurrection of human beings is simply impossible, then Christ Himself could not have risen from the grave. Since Jesus was truly human, what cannot happen to human beings could not have happened to Him.

If Christ never rose from the dead, the apostles' entire preaching is empty and meaningless. It also means the faith of believers is useless, because it would be placed in a false story. Everything in the Christian life depends on the truth of Jesus being alive.

In addition, the apostles would be proven to be liars who dishonored God by telling falsehoods about Him. They had boldly testified that God raised Jesus, so if the dead never rise, they made God look like a deceiver. The apostles had zero reason to invent such a story, which only brought them persecution.

Paul repeats the logical problem to drive the point home to his readers. If it is impossible for the dead to be raised, then Christ was not raised either. There is no middle ground between believing in bodily resurrection and believing in Christ.

If Christ remained in the grave, faith in Him cannot save anyone, and believers are still trapped under the guilt and punishment of their sins. The resurrection was God's public proof that Christ's sacrifice had paid the full penalty for human wrongdoing. Without that victory, no one has been reconciled to God.

If Jesus never rose, then Christians who have already died have completely perished. Their trust in Christ would have brought them no eternal life, and they would be lost forever in their sins. Denying the resurrection strips away all comfort for grieving believers.

If our hope in Christ only helps us during this earthly life, Christians are more to be pitied than anyone else. Believers endure trials, self-denial, and persecution for the sake of an eternal reward that would not exist. True Christian joy rests entirely on the reality of the life to come.

Paul triumphantly states the real truth: Christ has indeed been raised from the dead! In ancient Israel, the first part of a crop brought to God was called the firstfruits, which served as a guarantee of the full harvest to come. Christ's resurrection is that pledge, proving that everyone who belongs to Him will also rise.

God solved the problem of death in a way that matches how it started. Physical death entered the world through one human being, Adam, because of his rebellion. Therefore, the bodily resurrection from the dead also comes through one human being, Jesus Christ.

All human beings share in Adam's fallen nature and therefore experience physical death. In the exact same way, all who are united to Christ will be given bodily life through His resurrection power. Jesus completely undoes the curse brought by the fall.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand 'all will be made alive' to refer only to believers who are spiritually united to Christ.
Many evangelicals believe this teaches that every human being without exception will be physically resurrected by Christ, though only believers are raised to eternal life.

notes.meaning: The resurrection happens in a specific, orderly sequence, like troops marching in their assigned ranks. Christ marched first as the forerunner and pledge of the harvest. Then, when He returns in glory, all the believers who belong to Him will be raised to life.

After the resurrection of believers, the final completion of history will arrive. Christ will crush every opposing spiritual and earthly ruler that has fought against God. Once every rebel power is overthrown, Jesus will present the kingdom to God the Father.

differ.view: Premillennial Christians believe that between Christ's coming and the final end, He will reign on earth for a literal thousand years.
Many Reformed Christians believe Christ's reign is happening now from heaven during the church age, and 'the end' occurs when He returns to start the final eternal state.

notes.meaning: Christ must continue His reign as mediator until every single enemy has been brought completely under His power. Paul points to Psalm 110, where God promised that the Messiah would rule until His enemies become a footstool beneath His feet. This guarantees the final and total triumph of God's kingdom.

The final enemy that will be wiped out is physical death itself. When Christ raises His people from their graves, death will lose its grip on humanity and be destroyed forever. Sin and Satan are defeated first, and death is undone at the final resurrection.

Paul quotes Psalm 8 to show that God has placed all created things under Christ's feet. However, he clarifies that God the Father Himself is not placed under Jesus, since the Father is the One who gave the Son this universal authority. The Son's dominion is exercised in full harmony with the Father.

When all enemies are conquered and all creation is brought under Christ's rule, the Son will voluntarily place Himself under the Father who granted Him this task. This does not mean Jesus is less divine than the Father, for They share the same eternal nature. Rather, having accomplished the goal of saving creation, the Son presents the kingdom so that God may be all in all.

Paul points to people who were being baptized on behalf of dead loved ones. If the dead are never raised, undergoing this ritual makes no sense at all. Paul mentions this local custom to show the inconsistency of their doubts, without endorsing the practice itself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars think Paul refers to a local practice of people being baptized on behalf of friends who died before baptism, which Paul mentions to make his argument without endorsing it.
